ruling.quote: Transact Pro was preparing to open merchant accounts for the Apex Defendants at a third bank, Decta Limited

reason: New accounts are offered after earlier ones closed, which could be a replacement, but the complaint does not say the aim is that reports and history do not follow the seller.
The paragraphs describe thresholds, caps and processed totals in general terms. None gives a chargeback or return rate or count for any named account.
Accounts are opened under assumed names and merchant-client dbas, with false statements that hide who is really behind the account (Madera is said not to process for third parties).
Defendants run various third-party merchants' payments through accounts they hold, and conceal this from the banks, which is processing for others through one's own account.
Madera and B&P share a website and list the same residence on bank account applications (para 46), and those applications are the misrepresented ones that support T2 (para 63).
A closed Supplier Source account is restructured, re-opened and re-papered with a different signer, with the link to Apply Knowledge concealed, so that history does not follow the seller.

ruling.quote: if we move everything off PayPal, we'll send the PayPal account into severe chargeback state which will get reported to Visa

reason: Volume sits across PayPal and WorldPay and moving it would trigger Visa reporting, which could mean splitting, but the complaint does not say the split is to stay under thresholds.

ruling.quote: is a strong indication that the merchant applicant is “load balancing”

reason: The complaint calls identical paired accounts an indication of load balancing and quotes a third party's accusation, but does not itself allege these merchants split volume to avoid thresholds.

A billing descriptor was switched (para 75) and Nesch reopened under a different business name after a termination for chargebacks (paras 61, 91), over time and with a plain link to evading monitoring.

ruling.quote: A merchant with ten accounts, for example, could potentially accrue ten times the number of chargebacks

reason: Seven accounts follow a product-type policy and para 32 is a general point about thresholds. The complaint does not allege MOBE spread volume to stay under thresholds.

ruling.quote: claimed that MOBE, the DBA of MOBEProcessing.com Inc., was located in North Carolina, and not in Malaysia

reason: The wording on location and a signer with no ownership could mean false statements about who the seller is, but no straw owner or shell is alleged in so many words.

ruling.quote: The only possible way to take this somewhere else is to present it as new

reason: Moves of volume to other accounts or processors after closure are shown, but the only link to history is a stated plan to present MOBE as new, which was not carried out.
SLG's principals are alleged to use shell companies and frequently changing dba names, and AFTS posed the processor as its client when it knew the merchant was SLG.

ruling.quote: It pretended that its “client” was the processor (PAN and later RubikPay), which had the contractual relationship with SLG.

reason: Funds pass through a nested processor, which could mean sellers' sales run through another's account, but the complaint does not say several sellers share one account or whom AFTS misled.
Para 57 reports the NSL, NSP and SLS entities operating at the same address, and these are SLG dbas that support T2 as ruled.
Nexway moved charges from Adyen to Ingenico, a change of processor only. No name, descriptor or account of the seller changed, and no link to reports is stated.

ruling.quote: We would like to go over a plan to move volume back before starting.

reason: Moving volume between ACRO accounts to avoid scrutiny could mean splitting, but the paragraph does not say volume is spread to stay under a threshold.
Dangelmaier tells the owners to refund complainers at once so they do not file chargebacks and push thresholds too high, tying refunds to avoiding chargebacks.
Reimage is alleged to want accounts at Paddle to spread sales volume across more providers, a tactic of sellers expecting termination for chargeback risk, which links to monitoring.
Restoro Limited and Reimage Limited are alleged to be registered to straw owners or directors and not the actual owners.
PC Vark cycled through company names and Paddle changed billing descriptors so Visa could not see seller chargeback rates, which are changes over time so history does not follow the seller.
Para 63 alleges PC Vark's accounts share account contact information, but T1 and T2 here rest on Reimage (paras 102, 106) and para 63 does not tie the attribute to those accounts.

ruling.quote: Defendants advised Reimage to modify its credit card billing descriptor so as to avoid “suggest[ing] an unregistered [payfac] relationship” to the card networks.

reason: A descriptor change is advised to avoid network detection, but no change is alleged to have been made and the aim is hiding the payfac link, not history.

ruling.quote: the continuous supply of shell accounts was highly profitable for Humboldt, and it enabled the online scams that used them as fronts to avoid detection

reason: Closed accounts are followed by new shell accounts for avoiding detection, which could mean replacement, but the complaint does not say a closed seller's account was replaced so history would not follow.
